claim: Cathelicidin-MH (cath-MH) is a novel antimicrobial peptide from the skin of Microhyla heymonsivogt frog.
source: Here we report a new antimicrobial peptide belonging to the cathelicidin family, cathelicidin-MH (cath-MH), from the skin of Microhyla heymonsivogt frog.
evidence: The abstract directly states the identification of cath-MH from M. heymonsivogt frog skin.

claim: Cath-MH has a single α-helical structure in membrane-mimetic environments.
source: Cath-MH has a single α-helical structure in membrane-mimetic environments and is antimicrobial against fungi and bacteria, especially Gram-negative bacteria.
evidence: The abstract states this structural characteristic, supported by CD and X-ray crystallography data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cath-MH is antimicrobial against fungi and bacteria, especially Gram-negative bacteria.

claim: Cath-MH suppresses coagulation by affecting the enzymatic activities of tissue plasminogen activator, plasmin, β-tryptase, elastase, thrombin, and chymase.

claim: Cath-MH protects against lipopolysaccharide (LPS)- and cecal ligation and puncture-induced sepsis.

claim: The stabilization of the cath-MH α-helical monomer is provided by a disulfide bridge formed from sulfur atoms of C3 and C7.

evidence: This is stated based on structural analysis of the crystal structure.

claim: The cath-MH monomer is more positively charged at the N-terminus than the C-terminus.

claim: H2O-dissolved cath-MH presents negative peaks at 198 nm in CD spectra, suggesting the presence of a random coil structure.

evidence: This is stated based on CD spectroscopy data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Cath-MH dissolved in SDS solutions shows CD spectra with a large positive peak at 191 nm accompanied by two small negative peaks at 208 nm and 224 nm, suggesting an α-helix structure.
source: A large positive peak at 191 nm accompanied by two small negative peaks at 208 nm and 224 nm were observed in the CD spectra of cath-MH dissolved in SDS solutions, suggesting that the secondary structure of cath-MH contained an α-helix.
evidence: This is stated based on CD spectroscopy data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Different concentrations of SDS (30–120 mM) slightly change the secondary structure components of cath-MH.
source: Moreover, different concentrations of SDS (30–120 mM) slightly changed the secondary structure components of cath-MH.
evidence: This is stated based on CD spectroscopy data.

claim: The α-helix structure of cath-MH is preserved in CD spectra of 400 mM NaCl solution.
source: Dissolution in SDS solutions with NaCl varied the cath-MH CD spectra (Figure 2F), although the α-helix structure of cath-MH was preserved in CD spectra of 400 nM NaCl solution.
evidence: This is stated based on CD spectroscopy data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The secondary structure of cath-MH remains highly similar at different temperatures.
source: The secondary structure of the peptide remained highly similar at different temperatures (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is stated based on CD spectroscopy data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: LPS solutions can induce an α-helical secondary structure of cath-MH.
source: Interestingly, compared to the CD spectra seen with LPS solution or peptide dissolved in H2O, the characteristic α-helix peaks of cath-MH in the presence of 50 µM LPS were consistent with those seen in SDS solutions (Figure 2H), suggesting that LPS solutions could induce an α-helical secondary structure of cath-MH, which might be associated with its antimicrobial activity.
evidence: This is stated based on CD spectroscopy data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Cath-MH has broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity against all tested organisms.

claim: At 3× MIC, cath-MH successfully eliminates all viable E. coli ATCC 25922 colonies by 150 min.

evidence: This is stated based on bacterial killing kinetics data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Cath-MH is bactericidal rather than bacteriostatic.

claim: Cath-MH permeabilizes bacterial cells and disrupts membrane integrity.

source: Furthermore, the change in enthalpy (ΔH) of binding between cath-MH and LPS was −1.76 ± 0.93 kcal/mol.
evidence: This is stated based on ITC data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The ΔH of cath-MH binding to d-(+)-galacturonic acid is −3.01 ± 0.047 kcal/mol.
source: As shown in (Figure 4C), there was also heat release when the peptide bound to d-(+)-galacturonic acid (ΔH −3.01 ± 0.047 kcal/mol; Kd1.29 ± 0.144 µM).
evidence: This is stated based on ITC data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The Kd of cath-MH binding to d-(+)-galacturonic acid is 1.29 ± 0.144 µM as determined by ITC.
source: As shown in (Figure 4C), there was also heat release when the peptide bound to d-(+)-galacturonic acid (ΔH −3.01 ± 0.047 kcal/mol; Kd1.29 ± 0.144 µM).
evidence: This is stated based on ITC data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Binding of cath-MH to d-(+)-galacturonic acid saturates at about 10 min with a molar ratio of 6 (peptide to d-(+)-galacturonic acid).
source: Binding saturated at about 10 min with a molar ratio of 6 (peptide to d-(+)-galacturonic acid) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated based on ITC data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The Kd of cath-MH binding to LPS is about 2.81 µM as determined by SPRi.
source: The Kd values of cath-MH binding to LPS and d-(+)-galacturonic were about 2.81 µM and 4.52 µM, respectively, in agreement with the ITC results (Supplementary file 4; Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This is stated based on SPRi data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The Kd of cath-MH binding to d-(+)-galacturonic acid is about 4.52 µM as determined by SPRi.
source: The Kd values of cath-MH binding to LPS and d-(+)-galacturonic were about 2.81 µM and 4.52 µM, respectively, in agreement with the ITC results (Supplementary file 4; Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This is stated based on SPRi data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Cath-MH dose-dependently inhibits plasma coagulation.
source: Cath-MH dose-dependently inhibited plasma coagulation (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated based on plasma recalcification time data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Cath-MH at 0.4 μg/ml delays clotting to ~3 min.
source: Cath-MH increased the Ca2+ clotting time of normal human plasma in vitro, and even cath-MH at 0.4 μg/ml delayed clotting to ~3 min (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated based on plasma recalcification time data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Some plasma components can bind cath-MH.
source: As shown in Figure 5B, an intense SPRi signal was produced and the resonance unit increase was concentration dependent when three plasma concentrations were passed over chip-immobilized cath-MH, indicating that some plasma components can bind cath-MH.
evidence: This is inferred from SPRi data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: At 0.004 mg/ml, cath-MH significantly inhibits the enzymatic activities of tPA, plasmin, β-tryptase, elastase, and thrombin.
source: As shown in Figure 5C, at 0.004 mg/ml, cath-MH showed little or no activity against trypsin, FXIIa, FXIa, FXa, and kallikrein but significantly inhibited the enzymatic activities of tPA, plasmin, β-tryptase, elastase, and thrombin by 50.7%, 17.7%, 82.0%, 11.1%, and 8.6%, respectively.
evidence: This is stated based on enzyme inhibition assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Cath-MH increases the enzymatic activity of chymase, with remaining enzymatic activity of 341.5 ± 7.7%.
source: Interestingly, cath-MH increased the enzymatic activity of chymase, and its remaining enzymatic activity in the presence of cath-MH was 341.5 ± 7.7%.
evidence: This is stated based on enzyme inhibition assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The injection of 5 mg/kg cath-MH delays the bleeding time of mice for 5.34 min compared to the saline water control group.
source: In consistent with in vitro results, the injection of 5 mg/kg cath-MH delayed the bleeding time of mice for 5.34 min when compared the saline water control group (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated based on bleeding time data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The mortality rate in LPS-induced septic mice is 90% in the model group by the end of experiment.
source: Furthermore, the mortality rate was 90% in the model group by the end of experiment, while dexamethasone and cath-MH treatments successfully reduced LPS-induced mortality to 80% and 70%, respectively (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated based on survival data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Dexamethasone treatment reduces LPS-induced mortality to 80%.
source: Furthermore, the mortality rate was 90% in the model group by the end of experiment, while dexamethasone and cath-MH treatments successfully reduced LPS-induced mortality to 80% and 70%, respectively (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated based on survival data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Cath-MH treatment reduces LPS-induced mortality to 70%.
source: Furthermore, the mortality rate was 90% in the model group by the end of experiment, while dexamethasone and cath-MH treatments successfully reduced LPS-induced mortality to 80% and 70%, respectively (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated based on survival data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Treatment with cath-MH or dexamethasone 1 hr after LPS challenge markedly ameliorates abnormal histopathological changes in lungs, livers, and kidneys.
source: However, treatment with cath-MH or dexamethasone 1 hr after LPS challenge markedly ameliorated those abnormal histopathological changes and significantly decreased the injury scores in the lungs, livers, and kidneys compared to LPS administration alone (p<0.05) (Figure 6B,C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated based on histopathological data shown in Figures 6B, 6C, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The wet to dry lung weight ratio in the LPS model group increases dramatically compared to the control group.
source: In agreement, the wet to dry lung weight ratio in the model group increased dramatically in contrast to the control group, while cath-MH and dexamethasone obviously suppressed this increase compared to the model group (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is stated based on wet/dry ratio data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Cath-MH and dexamethasone suppress the increase in wet to dry lung weight ratio in LPS-induced septic mice.
source: In agreement, the wet to dry lung weight ratio in the model group increased dramatically in contrast to the control group, while cath-MH and dexamethasone obviously suppressed this increase compared to the model group (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is stated based on wet/dry ratio data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: MPO activity increases markedly in the LPS model group compared to the control group.
source: MPO activity also increased markedly in the model group compared to the control group and was significantly inhibited by cath-MH and dexamethasone (by 60.6 ± 5.5% and 94.5 ± 4.2%, respectively; Figure 6E).
evidence: This is stated based on MPO activity data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Cath-MH inhibits MPO activity by 60.6 ± 5.5% in LPS-induced septic mice.
source: MPO activity also increased markedly in the model group compared to the control group and was significantly inhibited by cath-MH and dexamethasone (by 60.6 ± 5.5% and 94.5 ± 4.2%, respectively; Figure 6E).
evidence: This is stated based on MPO activity data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Dexamethasone inhibits MPO activity by 94.5 ± 4.2% in LPS-induced septic mice.
source: MPO activity also increased markedly in the model group compared to the control group and was significantly inhibited by cath-MH and dexamethasone (by 60.6 ± 5.5% and 94.5 ± 4.2%, respectively; Figure 6E).
evidence: This is stated based on MPO activity data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Increases in gene expression and protein production of pro-inflammatory cytokines in different organs elicited by LPS are significantly inhibited by cath-MH and dexamethasone.
source: As shown in Figure 6F–K, Figure 6—figure supplements 2 and 3, increases in gene expression and protein production of pro-inflammatory cytokines in different organs elicited by LPS after 12 hr were significantly inhibited by cath-MH and dexamethasone, except for TNF-α protein production in livers.
evidence: This is stated based on cytokine measurement data shown in Figures 6F-K and Figure 6—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: Injection of LPS (25 mg/kg) significantly upregulates the expression of phosphorylated ERK, JNK, and p38 in lungs, livers, and kidneys.
source: Consistent with their effects on pro-inflammatory cytokine expression in lungs, livers, and kidneys, injection of LPS (25 mg/kg) significantly upregulated the expression of phosphorylated ERK, JNK, and p38 in all tested tissues.
evidence: This is stated based on western blot data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Treatment with cath-MH and dexamethasone suppresses LPS-induced increases in phosphorylated ERK, JNK, and p38 expression.
source: However, treatment with cath-MH and dexamethasone successfully suppressed these increases but had no influence on total ERK, JNK, and p38 expression.
evidence: This is stated based on western blot data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Cath-MH has a stronger inhibitory effect than dexamethasone on phosphorylated ERK, JNK, and p38 in kidneys, livers, and lungs.
source: Notably, cath-MH had a stronger inhibitory effect than dexamethasone on phosphorylated ERK, JNK, and p38 in kidneys, livers, and lungs.
evidence: This is stated based on western blot data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The mortality rate of cath-MH-treated CLP mice is 75% three days after operation.
source: The mortality rates of cath-MH-treated, CLP model, and sham control mice were 75%, 87.5%, and 0% three days after operation, respectively (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is stated based on survival data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The mortality rate of CLP model mice is 87.5% three days after operation.
source: The mortality rates of cath-MH-treated, CLP model, and sham control mice were 75%, 87.5%, and 0% three days after operation, respectively (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is stated based on survival data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The mortality rate of sham control mice is 0% three days after operation.
source: The mortality rates of cath-MH-treated, CLP model, and sham control mice were 75%, 87.5%, and 0% three days after operation, respectively (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is stated based on survival data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: CLP markedly increases alveolar wall thickness and inflammatory cell infiltration accompanied by destruction of the alveolar structures.
source: Compared with sham control mice, CLP markedly increased alveolar wall thickness and inflammatory cell infiltration accompanied by destruction of the alveolar structures and reductions in the alveolar spaces.
evidence: This is stated based on histopathological examination.

claim: Cath-MH alleviates CLP-induced lung pathological changes, showing well-preserved alveolar structures and less edema and hemorrhage.
source: However, these changes were alleviated by cath-MH, showing well-preserved alveolar structures and less edema and hemorrhage than untreated controls (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is stated based on histopathological data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Lung damage scores in the cath-MH-treated group are significantly lower than those in the CLP model group.
source: In the cath-MH-treated group, lung damage scores were significantly lower than those in the CLP model group (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is stated based on lung injury score data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The wet to dry lung weight ratio in the CLP model group is significantly higher than in the sham control group.
source: The wet to dry lung weight ratio in the CLP model group was significantly higher than in the sham control group. However, this increase was significantly inhibited, although not completely reversed, by cath-MH (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is stated based on wet/dry ratio data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Cath-MH significantly inhibits the increase in wet to dry lung weight ratio in CLP mice.
source: The wet to dry lung weight ratio in the CLP model group was significantly higher than in the sham control group. However, this increase was significantly inhibited, although not completely reversed, by cath-MH (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is stated based on wet/dry ratio data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: MPO activity is significantly increased in the CLP model group compared to the sham control group.
source: Consistently, MPO activity was significantly increased in the CLP model group compared to the sham control group. However, MPO activity was significantly lower in the cath-MH group compared to model mice (by 57.3 ± 2.6%; Figure 8E).
evidence: This is stated based on MPO activity data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Cath-MH reduces MPO activity by 57.3 ± 2.6% in CLP mice.
source: Consistently, MPO activity was significantly increased in the CLP model group compared to the sham control group. However, MPO activity was significantly lower in the cath-MH group compared to model mice (by 57.3 ± 2.6%; Figure 8E).
evidence: This is stated based on MPO activity data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α expression is significantly upregulated in CLP mice compared to sham controls.
source: Similarly, IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α expression was significantly upregulated in CLP mice compared those sham controls, and cath-MH significantly abrogated these increases (Figure 8F–K).
evidence: This is stated based on cytokine measurement data shown in Figures 8F-K.

claim: Cath-MH significantly abrogates the increases in IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α expression in CLP mice.
source: Similarly, IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α expression was significantly upregulated in CLP mice compared those sham controls, and cath-MH significantly abrogated these increases (Figure 8F–K).
evidence: This is stated based on cytokine measurement data shown in Figures 8F-K.

claim: Cath-MH has no hemolysis effect in red blood cells from mice with a hemolysis rate of 2.64 ± 1.40% at a concentration of 212.77 μg/ml.
source: The results showed that cath-MH had no hemolysis effect in red blood cells from mice and its hemolysis rate was 2.64 ± 1.40% at a concentration of 212.77 μg/ml.
evidence: This is stated based on hemolysis assay data.

claim: There are no significant differences in serum levels of AST, ALT, BUN, and Cr between control and cath-MH-treated mice after 24 hr and 48 hr inoculation.
source: As depicted in Figure 8—figure supplement 2B–E, there were no significant differences in serum levels of AST, ALT, BUN, and Cr between the two groups after 24 hr and 48 hr inoculation.
evidence: This is stated based on blood biochemical analysis data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2B-E.

claim: No significant histopathological changes are observed in tissues of lung, liver, and kidney between control and cath-MH-treated mice.
source: Furthermore, no significant histopathological changes were observed in tissues of lung, liver, and kidney between the control and cath-MH-treated mice (Figure 8—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is stated based on histopathological examination shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2F.

claim: The injected cath-MH dose of 10 mg/kg causes no or little acute toxicity to mice.
source: Therefore, the injected cath-MH dose, 10 mg/kg, caused no or little acute toxicity to mice, and there were no significant histopathological changes in tissues between the control and cath-MH-treated mice.
evidence: This is concluded based on toxicity assessment data.

claim: Septic shock is a life-threatening condition caused by systemic inflammatory responses to infection.
source: Septic shock is a life-threatening condition caused by systemic inflammatory responses to infection (Huang et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Huang et al., 2019.

claim: Multiorgan dysfunction or failure, including acute lung injury, is the most important pathological feature of sepsis.
source: Multiorgan dysfunction or failure, including acute lung injury, is the most important pathological feature of sepsis.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about sepsis.

claim: Sepsis has become a global health crisis and continues to be one of the main causes of death in intensive care units in developed countries.
source: Over the past few decades, despite significant advances in the development of antimicrobial therapies and management strategies, sepsis has become a global health crisis and continues to be one of the main causes of death in intensive care units in developed countries (Huang et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Huang et al., 2019.

claim: Some natural AMPs like cathelicidin with strong antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory activity may be excellent therapeutic candidates for sepsis.
source: There is increasing evidence that some natural AMPs like cathelicidin with strong antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory activity may be excellent therapeutic candidates for sepsis (Coorens et al., 2017; Giacometti et al., 2004; Hu et al., 2016; Murakami et al., 2009; Scott et al., 2002; Song et al., 2015; Qin et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Mature cath-MH assumes a primarily amphipathic α-helical structure in membrane-mimicking environments and LPS solutions.
source: Furthermore, CD and X-ray structural analyses showed that mature cath-MH assumes an primarily amphipathic α-helical structure in membrane-mimicking environments and LPS solutions, which is a common structural characteristic of most cathelicidins from tailless amphibians (Agier et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated based on CD and X-ray structural analyses, supported by a citation to Agier et al., 2015.

claim: Adopting a helical shape during membrane interactions allows unilateral segregation of hydrophobic residues and results in membrane penetration, transmembrane pore formation, and bacterial lysis.
source: Adopting such a helical shape during membrane interactions allows unilateral segregation of its hydrophobic residues and results in membrane penetration, transmembrane pore formation, and bacterial lysis (Dürr et al., 2006; Sancho-Vaello et al., 2017; Wei et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Circulating LPS induces extensive pro-inflammatory cytokine expression including TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6, which contribute to the pathophysiology of endotoxic shock.
source: As a trigger of inflammation and the dysregulated host response in sepsis (Salomao et al., 2012), circulating LPS is known to induce extensive pro-inflammatory cytokine expression including TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6, which contribute to the pathophysiology of endotoxic shock such as tissue injury, capillary leakage, circulatory failure, and multiorgan dysfunction (Van Amersfoort et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Salomao et al., 2012 and Van Amersfoort et al., 2003.

claim: Cath-MH can neutralize LPS and inactivate bacterial pathogens.
source: Like LL-37, OL-CATH2, Lf-CATH1, cathelicidin-PP, cathelicidin-PY, and cathelicidin-RC (Dürr et al., 2006; Ling et al., 2014; Mu et al., 2017; Qi et al., 2019; Wei et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2013), our compelling evidence demonstrates that cath-MH can neutralize LPS and inactivate bacterial pathogens.
evidence: This is stated based on experimental evidence, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Cath-MH particularly inhibits lung injury in LPS-induced septic mice.
source: Intriguingly, cath-MH particularly inhibited lung injury in LPS-induced septic mice, although it also had positive effects in other organs.
evidence: This is stated based on experimental data.

claim: Sepsis-induced lung dysfunction leads to the complete failure of other organs.
source: Previous studies have shown that sepsis-induced lung dysfunction leads to the complete failure of other organs (Matute-Bello et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Matute-Bello et al., 2008.

claim: CLP results in polymicrobial infection of the peritoneal cavity that can lead to sepsis, major organ failure, and death.
source: In addition, CLP results in polymicrobial infection of the peritoneal cavity that can lead to sepsis, major organ failure, and death (Rittirsch et al., 2009), and the inflammatory response in CLP septic mice is similar to that in patients with sepsis.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Rittirsch et al., 2009.

claim: The inflammatory response in CLP septic mice is similar to that in patients with sepsis.
source: In addition, CLP results in polymicrobial infection of the peritoneal cavity that can lead to sepsis, major organ failure, and death (Rittirsch et al., 2009), and the inflammatory response in CLP septic mice is similar to that in patients with sepsis.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Rittirsch et al., 2009.

claim: TLR signaling contributes to the secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines in endotoxic shock induced by LPS through activation of downstream MAPK signaling.
source: It is generally accepted that TLR signaling contributes to the secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines in endotoxic shock induced by LPS through activation of downstream MAPK signaling (Leifer and Medvedev, 2016; Salomao et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Leifer and Medvedev, 2016 and Salomao et al., 2012.

claim: The protective effect of cath-MH in experimental sepsis models is associated with LPS binding and the inhibition of pro-inflammatory cytokine production by blocking MAPK signaling.
source: Nevertheless, our results suggest that the protective effect of cath-MH in experimental sepsis models is associated with LPS binding and the inhibition of pro-inflammatory cytokine production by blocking MAPK signaling.
evidence: This is concluded based on experimental data.

claim: LL-37 displays low sequence identity with cath-MH and lacks loop2 at the C-terminus as well as a disulfide bridge at the N-terminus.
source: Although both LL-37 and cath-MH share high secondary structural similarity and can protect mice from lethal endotoxic shock, LL-37 displays low sequence identity with cath-MH and lacks loop2 at the C-terminus as well as a disulfide bridge at the N-terminus (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated based on sequence and structural comparison shown in Figure 1D.

claim: More residues in cath-MH are extended in the C-terminus of the disulfide bridge compared to other known cathelicidins from frogs.
source: In addition, different to any other known cathelicidins from frogs, more residues in cath-MH are extended in the C-terminus of the disulfide bridge and the KVKQ sequence is in the interval between the conserved K10 and KIK16 residues.
evidence: This is stated based on sequence comparison.

claim: Cath-MH contains a larger helix and five extra hydrogen bonds compared to cathelicidin-PY.
source: Finally, compared to cathelicidin-PY (Wei et al., 2013), cath-MH contains a larger helix and five extra hydrogen bonds.
evidence: This is stated based on structural comparison, supported by a citation to Wei et al., 2013.

claim: Sepsis is almost invariably associated with coagulation abnormalities that facilitate the recruitment of profibrinolytic enzymes such as uPA, tPA, and plasmin.
source: Sepsis is almost invariably associated with coagulation abnormalities that facilitate the recruitment of profibrinolytic enzymes such as uPA, tPA, and plasmin (Gould et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Gould et al., 2015.

claim: A lack of human chymase and its homolog in mouse mast cells can increase FXIIIA expression and activity and decrease bleeding time during sepsis.
source: In addition, a lack of human chymase and its homolog in mouse mast cells can increase FXIIIA expression and activity and decrease bleeding time during sepsis.
evidence: This is a statement about the role of chymase in sepsis.

claim: Fibrinolytic enzymes and chymase closely correlate with disease severity and fatality in sepsis.
source: Therefore, fibrinolytic enzymes and chymase closely correlate with disease severity and fatality in sepsis (Zeerleder et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Zeerleder et al., 2007.

claim: Neutrophil elastase is associated with pulmonary endothelial injury under LPS-induced endotoxemic conditions.
source: Furthermore, neutrophil elastase is associated with pulmonary endothelial injury under LPS-induced endotoxemic conditions (Suzuki et al., 2019), and inhibitors such as sivelestat can attenuate sepsis-related acute tissue injury (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Suzuki et al., 2019 and Li et al., 2016.

claim: Inhibitors such as sivelestat can attenuate sepsis-related acute tissue injury.
source: Furthermore, neutrophil elastase is associated with pulmonary endothelial injury under LPS-induced endotoxemic conditions (Suzuki et al., 2019), and inhibitors such as sivelestat can attenuate sepsis-related acute tissue injury (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2016.

claim: β-tryptase promotes early pulmonary fibrosis in sepsis-induced lung injury.
source: Finally, β-tryptase promotes early pulmonary fibrosis in sepsis-induced lung injury and anti-tryptase treatment has a therapeutic effect in experimental colitis (Isozaki et al., 2006; Villar et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Isozaki et al., 2006 and Villar et al., 2015.

claim: Anti-tryptase treatment has a therapeutic effect in experimental colitis.
source: Finally, β-tryptase promotes early pulmonary fibrosis in sepsis-induced lung injury and anti-tryptase treatment has a therapeutic effect in experimental colitis (Isozaki et al., 2006; Villar et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Isozaki et al., 2006 and Villar et al., 2015.

claim: Inhibiting coagulation with anticoagulants like antithrombin is beneficial for patients with severe infection and sepsis in experimental and initial clinical trials.
source: Furthermore, inhibiting coagulation with anticoagulants like antithrombin is beneficial for patients with severe infection and sepsis in experimental and initial clinical trials (Levi and van der Poll, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Levi and van der Poll, 2017.

claim: Cath-MH forms aggregates and stable dimers in solution and lipid bilayers.
source: Cath-MH forms aggregates and stable dimers in solution and lipid bilayers (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated based on structural analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Cath-MH is protected from proteolytic degradation, similar to LL-37.
source: Therefore, unlike other AMPs, it is protected from proteolytic degradation, similar to LL-37, the only cathelicidin peptide in humans, cleaved from a human cationic antimicrobial polypeptide of 18 kDa (hCAP18) (Dürr et al., 2006).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural properties of cath-MH, supported by a citation to Dürr et al., 2006.

claim: Synthetic LL-37 is rapidly degraded in periodontitis gingival crevicular fluid.
source: Nevertheless, synthetic LL-37 is rapidly degraded in periodontitis gingival crevicular fluid, restricting its application as a potential therapeutic in the gingival crevice (McCrudden et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to McCrudden et al., 2013.

claim: In purified human lung mast cells, β-tryptase rapidly cleaves LL-37.
source: In purified human lung mast cells, β-tryptase rapidly cleaves LL-37 (Schiemann et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Schiemann et al., 2009.

claim: Cath-MH is likely to have advantages over LL-37 as an anti-sepsis molecule because it inhibits or activates proteases.
source: Since it inhibits or activates proteases, cath-MH is likely to have advantages over LL-37 as an anti-sepsis molecule.
evidence: This is inferred from the protease inhibition/activation properties of cath-MH.

claim: Cath-MH may serve as a potent potential therapeutic agent for sepsis.
source: Taken together, multi-functional cath-MH may serve as a potent potential therapeutic agent for sepsis.
evidence: This is concluded based on all the experimental data presented in the manuscript.
